cohorts.summary: Early players struggle with slippery movement and imprecise controls.

claims.claim: Controls feel slippery, finicky, and imprecise, with nebulous attack ranges.

citations.review_text:
I'm 1.6 hours in. Given how hyped this game was and, being an enjoyer of "Metroidvanias," I expected to be drawn into this way more than I have been thus far. Perhaps it's my fault for starting the game on hard, but the enemies and attack system make combat annoying. Sure the game looks nice, but the graphics make it uniquely difficult to detect enemy attacks. I often feel like I'm getting hit by nothing. Given how hard enemies hit at this difficulty, the lack of accessible save points makes it even more annoying.

The combat reminds me of why Hollow Knight was so good - the combat felt precise, for one thing. Here, the controls are so slippery and the attack ranges so nebulous that it's hard to see why this is considered a masterpiece.

To me, graphics are the least important part of a game and the gameplay has felt so bad so far that they story is irrelevant.
The controls are too finicky and imprecise.

I only lasted 75 minutes. The story is mediocre, the gameplay is frustratingly simple, boring, or randomly full of instant kill things that make the save system that is resource based (the same resource you need for blowing up necessary obstacles to progress in the game) absolutely awful. Some praise its platforming. I found it slippery and tedious, barely difficult, mostly designed to be exactly Ori's jump height or distance. (at least within the first two areas of the game.) I heard the second game improves upon these things so I'm skipping this one to give the other a shot.

single_points.text: One reviewer says the game still doesn't map properly to a PS4 controller and Steam's system to emulate an Xbox controller doesn't work.

citation.review_text:
The game really does look beautiful, but it constantly opens on a secondary screen no matter how I change settings and it still doesn't map properly to a PS4 controller. Normally if a game doesn't support PS4 controllers but does support Xbox controllers I can use Steam's system to emulate an Xbox controller. But on this game that doesn't work and it ends up mapping the controls incorrectly. For example: A should = X, B should = O  In this game A = ▢ and B = X

So the game is unplayable on a PS4 controller, in a way that is uniquely bad and probably more effort to fix than the game is worth.

cohorts.summary: Players find the manual save system and basic combat balanced by stunning design, though visual clarity and vsync can cause friction.

claims.claim: Reviewers describe the save system as relying on a manual soul link mechanism that requires frequent saving to avoid losing progress upon death.

citations.review_text:
Ori is a great and visually appealing game. I really enjoyed the story and the gameplay too. It is smooth and fluid. Every new location brings something new and refreshes the gameplay, keeping distance from repetitiveness. Unique areas, backgrounds and enemies everywhere. The game is very good, but I do have something negative to say about this game.

I have played the second game (Will of the Wisps) first before playing Blind Forest. Obviously I expected the game to be different, since it's not only the prequel but also over 10 years old. But what caught me off guard is the save system. There is almost no autosave going on, except when entering a fight or an escape sequence. The only way to save your game is to "soul link" using energy.

Using energy isn't the problem at all, but the need to do this VERY often. I have continuously experienced the same thing - finally making a bit of progress and then accidentally dying, resulting in the game sending me way back to my last soul link and losing a lot of progress (often after finishing a hard or time consuming section). This has proven VERY frustrating. Yes, you could say it's my fault for not saving - you would be absolutely right, but do you really want to save every 5 minutes just to make sure you don't lose any progress? I don't think so. This is the only negative thing I have to say about Blind Forest.

My overall rating: 8/10

TLDR: Great and visually appealing game, but the save system could be improved.
edit: typos

How does one make such a jaw-droppingly beautiful game with buttery smooth movement, yet fuck up combat and specific basic mechanics so much? The game is near Pixar levels of gorgeous and the platforming is unique and challenging enough to be engaging that frankly, I feel like they should've exclusively made the game about the platforming rather than add some shoe-horned in combat. I was honestly shocked by how poor the combat was seeing as the solo developer of one of the best Metroidvanias in history(AM2R) worked on this game. The save system in this game is also a little dumb. Their answer to poor balancing of the platforming challenge at certain points is to essentially add a built in save-scumming feature. It's not a game-ruiner, but I think just balancing the gameplay enough to work with traditional saves would've been the better call. Otherwise, this is still definitely worth playing if you like the genre and I'm hoping the sequel is as fantastic as people say it is.

citations.review_text:
I originally played this around 10 years ago when it was fairly new, and I remember loving it back then. After replaying it I’m happy to see that it holds up extremely well. 

I had forgotten how difficult the game can be on just Normal, but I’d say 99% of my deaths were fair and just a skill issue. There are occasional times when it’s hard to see if a certain space is safe to walk on, or if an enemy projectile is actually an experience orb or not, and that can be annoying. Really though, it’s a credit to how beautiful the game looks, and art direction just takes a slight priority over gameplay practicality in a few spots. 

I love Metroidvanias and Ori is still one of the best. The movement and abilities are satisfying to chain together, and exploration feels intuitive  and fun. The famous/infamous “escape” sequences are challenging but super fun. The story is simple but effective, and as I mentioned before the visuals are absolutely stunning. I’m excited to finally play the second game soon.

As a side note, it runs beautifully on the Steam Deck, but turn off Vsync for slightly better performance.

A fun platformer metroidvania. It's not perfect but still fun. As good as the visuals are it does lead to a lot of visual noise that can make it difficult to see hazards, including combat when your only method for attack are bright fireballs. The game being primarily a platformer can make things a little frustrating with random oneshots.

citations.review_text: The visuals are amazing, the movement is good, the combat is very lacking compared to the sequel to this game. I give this game 8/10, while the sequel is 11/10 and one of my all time favorites.

I had a lot of technical problems with [i]Ori and the Blind Forest[/i] that are hard to separate from my actual experience. The game was a stuttery mess, and despite numerous forum 'fixes' it remained so for the entirety of my run.

For a platformer, that's not exactly a fair environment.

I absolutely hated the movement. It felt floaty and inconsistent with a delay to any action. It felt weighty when the character very clearly is not. Nothing required particular precision, but it just didn't feel nice. 

Again though, how do I divorce that from stutter? It probably was most of the cause!

Something that wasn't, though, was the combat. Button-mashing in my cute platformer is not fun, and I would have preferred that the enemies were just pure blocks that require you to use some sort of ability to get around them, like the [i]Sonic[/i] games. This actually is possible later in the game, and it's an immediate improvement to game flow. Combat added nothing.

The level design of [i]Ori[/i] was fine enough, albeit simple and somehow rather linear, due to too-frequent gating. Where it excels is its set pieces - escape sequences with stronger platforming challenges and great music. These sequences are the best part of [i]Ori[/i] and show an ability to create engagingly paced sections, but for whatever reason this level of quality isn't present in the rest of the game. I suppose the novelty would wear off eventually, but aspects, such as increased level complexity, should have been a default.

I do think I'm being a bit harsh with [i]Ori[/i]. High-fidelity platformers regained popularity after a long hiatus with this game as the start, and obviously what comes after would be a bit better. Still, is it worth your time? [i]Ori[/i] at least is short - this works to its benefit.
the games's really beautiful, combat mechanics are very dull but the movement mechanics are quite fun, not a bad game at all

I bought Ori and the Blind Forest years ago and kept waiting for the right moment to finally play it. That moment eventually came, and I finished the entire game in just a handful of sessions.

I should probably start by saying that I am not usually a huge fan of metroidvanias. I dislike excessive backtracking, and I am honestly tired of the pixel-art style that so many modern games in the genre seem to rely on.
That said, I loved almost every moment of it. The soundtrack is sublime, the art direction is gorgeous, and the whole experience feels like a fairy tale. It is one of those games where simply moving through the world can be satisfying because of how beautiful everything looks and sounds.

The weakest part is probably the combat. Fighting regular enemies and minibosses is fairly basic and sometimes even a little rough. Fortunately, the game is short enough that it never became especially frustrating for me.
The actual boss encounters are a completely different story. They are much more dynamic and interesting, and they are often among the most visually impressive moments in the game. Exploration is also very smooth and enjoyable, and moving through the world generally feels natural rather than tedious.

You can definitely tell that this was the studio's first game. A lot of its systems feel rough and relatively simple, but you can also tell how much care went into making it. There is a very clear sense of passion behind the music, the visuals, the environments and the overall presentation.
Overall, a splendid little gem, definitely worth the money and the time.

A pure platformer with good level design. the "bosses" are escape sequences requiring precise movement. very shallow combat mechanics, but this game does a great job of not overstaying its welcome. 8.7/10

I’m not gonna. You play it.

Movement. That’s the name of the game. I can’t imagine such a critter would move so smoothly. Ori’s movement allows you to express yourself through gameplay and it’s incredibly satisfying. 

A minor critique is the lackluster combat system of using The Orb™ to blast your enemies. It has since been corrected in their sequel.

citation.review_text:
Cute game.
Overall It's a pretty chill 2D platformer.
Though I think the pace at which you get abilities early on is a tad slow, which isn't helped by what feels like the most sadistic progression gate in the entire game being pretty early on.

Notes in random order
1. You need to lock your monitor to 60 FPS.
If you do not, the game's pace will continuously fluctuate between hypermode and slowmode - this will throw you off.
I did not try 120Hz.
2. Cheevos don't work
Can see my profile - nearly 100%'d it and got 0 cheevos for it.
3. The controls are pretty intuitive, except for stomp which kept activating when I was trying to glide.

[spoiler]
As for the early progression gate, you'll have about 2 abilities and MAYBE dash if you cleared that path first. There's a rock you can drag between a map stone and some thorns.
You cannot just push it to cover the thorns, you need to push it [b]beyond[/b] so it goes on an angle before your jump can reach and progression to the next area is possible.

It is the most sadistic progression gate in the entire game.
[/spoiler]

citations.review_text: A nice platforming vania. It takes a little while to get used to the MC's movements, so your first playthrough may be a bit frustrating. However, once you get used to the movement cycle, the game becomes very enjoyable. There is a wide variety of levels with unique mechanics, puzzles, fast-paced platforming, and fun escape sequences. Combat isn't that important in this game, but there are a lot of "gotcha" moments, so you'll quickly learn to practice patience!

People who complain about Silksong being difficult have NOT played this game, seriously.
I like the difficulty however, and even got all the achievements.

The game is relatively short, at around 7-8 hours if going for 100%, but I could consistently speedrun it in under 2 hours otherwise.

It's not a perfect game, since the combat is lacking, there are performance issues on newer hardware, and some of the achievements are bugged.
However the platforming, music, level design, story, and visuals are all top notch, making this one of my favorite games of all time.

single_points.text: One reviewer says the engine and the unpredictability of Ori's moves cause issues because Unity is notorious for messing up pinpoint moves due to how its physics work, especially on walls.

citation.review_text:
I love Metroidvanias and platformers but what I love more, is a game that blends in a beautiful art style with said genres. The world-building and storytelling of the game is immaculate. The developers magnificently managed to create a memorable map with unique areas that have their own quirks and challenges.

While this game may be old, the mechanics don't show its age at all. I was awestruck by abilities like Bash and Charge Jump and how new they were for me, even though this game is from 11 years ago.

The only downside of the game is the engine and the unpredictability of Ori's moves. That's not something to pin on the creators, however, as this game was made with Unity which is notorious for messing up pinpoint moves due to how its physics work, especially on walls. I've heard that the Definitive Edition fixed many similar issues.

All in all, a must play for fans of this genre.
